Before you start

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can tell high standards apart from the fear of mistakes, set a done line on one real task, and pick a small mistake experiment if they want to try one. Nobody shares grades or scores.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 4 minSound familiar? Stand up, sit down
  2. 6 minTwo parts: the standards and the fear
  3. 4 minIt isn’t only you: the rise
  4. 5 minGood enough is fine here: turn and talk, share out
  5. 10 minWhich thought is the trap? Claire, Nico, Alex
  6. 6 minSet a done line
  7. 4 minA mistake experiment, if you want
  8. 6 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Sound familiar, the two parts, the rise, one trap, the done line, and a mistake experiment.

Before you teach
Nobody shares grades or scores.

Keep to the examples on the slides. Don't ask what anyone got, where they're applying, or how they compare. In a small advisory, students already know a lot about each other's classes and results.

Keep the stand-up items light.

Use the five in the notes. Staying seated is always fine, and don't comment on who stood. Leave out food, bodies and sleep loss as items, because standing for those can single someone out.

Watch for the heavier signs, without screening.

The student page names restricting food, over-exercising, or hurting yourself when things aren't perfect as reasons to get help. Don't ask about these in the circle. If a student says something that worries you, thank them, follow up privately, and connect them with a counselor the same day.

Don't make it about blaming families.

The 2022 research on parents' expectations is a correlation. Many students feel love and pressure from the same people. Let both be true, and keep the "where does it come from" question private.

Not everyone in the circle is chasing a 94.

Some students are working hard to pass, and talk about "easing up" can sound like it's meant for other people. The done line and grading the process help with any grade. Keep examples about effort and time rather than high scores.

Model it if you can.

A quick, true example of your own done line, or a mistake that turned out fine, helps more than a lecture. Keep it short and low stakes.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

First to go to college, or carrying a family's sacrifice.

For some students a grade holds a family's move to this country, years of hard work, or being the first to go to college. Honor that. Present "talk about how much you're carrying" as an option, never as pushing back on family.

One of the only people like you in the class.

Students of color, and others who feel watched in advanced classes, may feel a mistake reflects on more than themselves. Name that pressure as real and partly outside their control, and keep the done line about what is in their control.

Expectations come from different adults.

The "have to" voice might belong to a single parent, a grandparent, an older sibling, a coach, or the student. Say "the adults in your life" or "family" rather than "your parents."

Learning differences and attention.

Students with a learning plan, ADHD, or slower processing may already spend longer on everything, so a time limit can feel unfair. Let them define what finished looks like first and set the time second. Avoid calling anyone "so OCD" about their work.

Time and money aren't equal.

Some students work a job, care for siblings, or can't pay for a tutor. Office hours and asking a teacher are free. Don't treat a summer internship or paid program as the standard; Claire's card is one example among many.

Gender expectations.

Some students feel they have to look flawless, and others feel they have to look effortless and never show they tried. Both come from the fear side. Mix genders in your examples and don't treat either as a girls' or boys' problem.

What the research says

Researchers split perfectionism into strivings (high standards and hard work) and concerns (fear of mistakes, doubt, and the sense that people only accept you if you're flawless). Later studies support parts of this model, not all of it.

Gaudreau and Thompson, Personality and Individual Differences, 2010

On their own, high personal standards tend to go with motivation and good outcomes.

Stoeber and Otto, Personality and Social Psychology Review, 2006

Socially prescribed perfectionism, the belief that other people demand perfection from you, is one of three types, along with perfectionism aimed at yourself and at others.

Hewitt and Flett, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1991

Across 41,641 college students in the U.S., Canada and the U.K. from 1989 to 2016, all three types of perfectionism rose. The sense that others demand perfection rose most, by about 33%.

Curran and Hill, Psychological Bulletin, 2019

Students' sense of their parents' expectations and criticism also rose over those decades and tracked with perfectionism. It's a correlation; the authors point to more competitive, higher-stakes environments.

Curran and Hill, Psychological Bulletin, 2022

A review of 284 studies linked perfectionism to depression, anxiety, OCD, eating disorders and self-harm, which is why therapists treat it as a risk factor across many problems.

Limburg, Watson, Hagger and Egan, Journal of Clinical Psychology, 2017
